prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not give corticosteroids before CSF cytology and flow cytometry, or before tissue is obtained when a biopsy is planned: steroids can make CNS lymphoma non-diagnostic
Do not pursue resection of a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before the non-invasive work-up (lesion pattern, CSF, AQP4/MOG serology) and, if needed, a stereotactic biopsy
Do not diagnose CNS lupus on a low-titre ANA with negative anti-dsDNA and ENA and no systemic features
Do not treat the lesion as an acute ischaemic stroke: there is no central restricted diffusion, and it enhances with an open ring
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS with a tumefactive lesion by the 2024 McDonald criteria: DIS in 3 of 5 regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, spinal cord) completed by DIT (enhancing and non-enhancing lesions) and positive CSF (three restricted oligoclonal bands, raised kFLC index), with the right face and arm numbness 15 months ago as an earlier attack, once CSF cytology and flow cytometry and the imaging make lymphoma unlikely.

Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3-5 days only after CSF cytology and flow cytometry are negative and MR spectroscopy favours demyelination; stop ibuprofen during the pulse or add gastric protection; plasma exchange if there is no response.
Repeat gadolinium MRI within 4-8 weeks to confirm regression of the tumefactive lesion; atypical evolution or no response prompts stereotactic biopsy.
Advise her not to drive until formal visual field testing shows that the left homonymous hemianopia meets the driving standard.
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (a tumefactive enhancing lesion and an earlier attack), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.
Before an anti-CD20 antibody or S1P modulator, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already negative) and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before the first dose.
Replace vitamin D (25-hydroxy vitamin D 14 ng/mL).

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure or paroxysmal event; an EEG does not help characterise the lesion.
A non-contrast head CT has already shown the lesion before admission; another CT adds radiation and nothing that the MRI does not give.
No murmur, fever or embolic pattern; a tumefactive lesion with ovoid lesions elsewhere is not an embolic picture.
No palpitations, syncope or cardiac history; rhythm monitoring does not inform a demyelinating lesion.
MRI pattern, CSF cytology and flow cytometry and MR spectroscopy address the lymphoma and glioma question; FDG-PET adds cost without changing management at this stage.

mri.impression: 1. 4.2 cm right parieto-occipital white matter lesion extending to the splenium, with incomplete (open) ring enhancement open toward the cortex, peripheral restricted diffusion along the enhancing margin, intralesional veins, surrounding oedema and mild compression of the right trigone without midline shift. 2. Three non-enhancing ovoid lesions: two periventricular (left frontal horn, right ventricular body) and one left parietal juxtacortical. The open-ring pattern and the additional ovoid lesions are most consistent with a tumefactive demyelinating lesion; a neoplasm, including lymphoma, cannot be excluded on imaging alone.

clinical_pearls: Open-ring enhancement with the opening facing the cortex favours a demyelinating lesion over neoplasm or abscess
Most people with a biopsy-proven tumefactive demyelinating lesion go on to relapsing MS, usually with typical lesions afterwards
A positive low-titre ANA alone does not establish CNS lupus; anti-dsDNA, ENA and complement and the clinical picture decide
MR spectroscopy with modest choline elevation favours demyelination over high-grade glioma but does not exclude lymphoma
A homonymous hemianopia from a retrochiasmal lesion leaves acuity and colour vision normal; a monocular deficit points to the optic nerve
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: a tumefactive lesion causing a left homonymous hemianopia mimics a tumour, an outside CT raised stroke, and a positive ANA with a mother with SLE adds a distractor. The diagnosis rests on the open-ring pattern, other typical lesions, a cord lesion, CSF oligoclonal bands with negative cytology and flow cytometry, and negative AQP4/MOG serology.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion overlapping neoplasm, abscess and infarct on imaging; the agent must exclude lymphoma before steroids, count DIS in three regions with DIT and CSF, and set aside the ANA and the outside CT.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lucia Vega is a 29-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman who presents to the emergency department with a five-day history of progressive left-sided visual field loss. She reports that she first noticed difficulty seeing objects to her left while driving home from work five days ago, initially thinking her glasses were smudged. Over the next 24 hours, the visual deficit became more pronounced and she began having difficulty reading text on her computer screen, missing words on the left side of the page. She also developed a bifrontal headache that she describes as a constant dull pressure, rated 5 out of 10 in severity, which is different in character from her typical migraines. The headache has been accompanied by mild photophobia. She denies any associated nausea, vomiting, or phonophobia. She has no history of similar visual symptoms. She reports that approximately fifteen months ago she experienced a two-week episode of numbness and tingling involving the right side of her face and right arm that resolved spontaneously. She attributed this to work-related stress and did not seek medical evaluation at the time. She denies any recent head trauma, fevers, chills, weight loss, joint pains, oral ulcers, or skin rashes. She denies any recent travel or sick contacts. Her primary care physician referred her to the emergency department after an urgent noncontrast CT scan of the head showed a hypodense area in the right parieto-occipital region with surrounding edema, raising concern for acute ischemia versus a mass lesion. Given her age and the acute presentation, she was admitted for further workup. On review of systems, she endorses mild fatigue over the past several months but denies any limb weakness, difficulty walking, urinary or bowel dysfunction, or swallowing difficulties. Her mother has systemic lupus erythematosus.
